Let $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with absolute value in the real
case and modulus $|a+ib|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ in the complex case. A scalar
sequence here is a function $x:\mathbb N\to\mathbb K$, including index zero. Let

$$\ell^\infty=\{x=(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}:\text{there is }C\ge0\text{ with }|x_n|\le C\text{ for all }n\},\qquad c_0=\{x\in\ell^\infty:x_n\to0\},$$

both equipped with $\|x\|_\infty=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}|x_n|$.  Thus $c_0$ is
a specified linear subspace of the bounded-sequence space $\ell^\infty$.

For each bounded sequence, the nonempty real set $\{|x_n|:n\in\mathbb N\}$
has a finite supremum by [[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]. This proves that
the displayed norm exists, rather than presuming existence in the definition
of boundedness. Its uniqueness requires no choice of supremum witnesses.

Here $x_n\to0$ means that for every real $\varepsilon>0$ there is
$N\in\mathbb N$ such that $|x_n|<\varepsilon$ for all $n\ge N$.
Addition and scalar multiplication are coordinatewise. The scalar triangle
inequality makes bounded sequences and null sequences linear spaces and gives
the triangle inequality for the displayed supremum norm. Absolute homogeneity
follows coordinatewise, and a zero supremum forces every coordinate to vanish.

For either scalar field $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, the space
$c_0(\mathbb K)$ with the supremum norm is a Banach space.  No choice
principle is used.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

Thus the coordinate formula is linear and $\|U(t)x\|_\infty\le\|x\|_\infty.$ If $x\in c_0$ and $\varepsilon>0$, choose $N$ so that $|x_j|<\varepsilon$ for all $j\ge N$; then $|(U(t)x)_j|\le|x_j|<\varepsilon$ for $j\ge N$. So $U(t)x\in c_0$, $U(t)$ is bounded, and [F6] gives $\|U(t)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le1$.

Since $\exp(0)=1$, $U(0)=I_X$. For $s,t\ge0$, [F3] gives $U(t)U(s)x=(\exp(-j^2t)\exp(-j^2s)x_j)_j =(\exp(-j^2(t+s))x_j)_j=U(t+s)x.$ Thus the semigroup identities hold on every coordinate and hence on $X$.

Fix $x\in X$, $t_0\ge0$, and $\varepsilon>0$. By [F1], choose $N$ such that $|x_j|<\varepsilon/3$ for $j\ge N$. For those indices, $|\exp(-j^2t)-\exp(-j^2t_0)|\,|x_j|<\varepsilon/3$ for every $t\ge0$, because both exponential factors lie in $[0,1]$. For the finitely many indices $j<N$, continuity in [F4] supplies a common $\delta>0$ such that the same coordinate differences are below $\varepsilon/3$ whenever $t\ge0$ and $|t-t_0|<\delta$. Taking the supremum over all coordinates proves $\|U(t)x-U(t_0)x\|_\infty<\varepsilon$. Therefore every orbit is continuous, so $U$ is strongly continuous.

The boundedness in step 1.1 holds for every $t$, so for each $T>0$, $\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|U(t)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le1.$ Together with the Banach property [F2], the semigroup identities in step 2.1, and strong continuity in step 2.2, this proves the statement.

Fix a scalar field $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. A **common-space
linear IVP interface** consists of a Banach space $X$ over $\mathbb K$ and a
strongly continuous semigroup $U(t)\in\mathcal B(X)$, $t\ge0$, as defined in
[[def-strongly-continuous-semigroup]], together with a finite-time bound: for
each $T>0$ there is $M_T<\infty$ such that
$$\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|U(t)\|\le M_T.$$
The solution with initial value $x\in X$ is $u(t)=U(t)x$. This definition
records the solution operators and their continuous dependence in the same
norm; it makes no claim about a generator domain.

A **consistency subspace** is a dense linear subspace $D\subseteq X$ satisfying
$U(t)D\subseteq D$ for every $t\ge0$. Here dense means
$\overline D^{\,X}=X$, and invariant means the displayed inclusion. It need
not be the domain of a differential generator.

A **common-space time-scheme family** is a sequence of positive time steps
$(\tau_\nu)_{\nu\in\mathbb N}$ with $\tau_\nu\to0$ and bounded linear maps
$S_\nu:X\to X$ in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. Write
$S_\nu^0=I_X$ and recursively set $S_\nu^{n+1}=S_\nu S_\nu^n$ for
$n\in\mathbb N$. These powers are uniquely defined by the recursion theorem
([[thm-recursion]]) on the set $\mathcal B(X)$ of bounded linear operators
([[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]): for fixed $S_\nu$, the map
$T\mapsto S_\nu T$ preserves $\mathcal B(X)$ because composition preserves
linearity and multiplies operator bounds, and $I_X\in\mathcal B(X)$ with bound
$1$. All scheme and solution errors below
use the norm of this same space $X$; write $\|\cdot\|$ for that norm and
$\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ for the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm]].

The family is **consistent on $D$** when for every $x\in D$ and $T>0$,
$$\lim_{\nu\to\infty}\max_{\substack{r\in\mathbb N\\r\tau_\nu\le T}}\frac{\|(S_\nu-U(\tau_\nu))U(r\tau_\nu)x\|}{\tau_\nu}=0.$$
The maximum is over a nonempty finite set because it includes $r=0$. This is
the local defect divided by one time step, uniformly over the exact orbit on
the finite time interval.

The family is **stable on finite time intervals** when for every $T>0$ there
is $C_T<\infty$ such that
$$\|S_\nu^n\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le C_T\quad\text{whenever }\nu,n\in\mathbb N\text{ and }n\tau_\nu\le T.$$
It is **convergent on finite time intervals** when for every $x\in X$ and
$T>0$,
$$\lim_{\nu\to\infty}\max_{\substack{n\in\mathbb N\\n\tau_\nu\le T}}\|S_\nu^n x-U(n\tau_\nu)x\|=0.$$
The maximum convention includes time zero. This locally uniform-in-grid-time
convergence is the hypothesis used for the reverse implication in the
equivalence theorem below.

Assume DC. Let $X$ be a Banach space, $Y$ a normed space, and let $\mathcal F$ be a family of bounded linear operators $X\to Y$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). If $\sup_{T\in\mathcal F}\|Tx\|<\infty$ for every $x\in X$, then $\sup_{T\in\mathcal F}\|T\|<\infty$, where the norm is [[def-operator-norm]].

The set of **natural numbers** is the **smallest inductive set**
([[def-inductive-set]]),

$$\mathbb{N} = \omega := \bigcap\,\{\, I : I \text{ is inductive} \,\},$$

which exists and is itself inductive by [[lem-omega-smallest-inductive]] (the
Axiom of Infinity, [[def-axiom-of-infinity]], supplies one inductive set to
intersect within, and Separation, [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]], makes the
intersection a set). On $\mathbb{N}$ we take

$$0 := \varnothing, \qquad \sigma(n) := n \cup \{n\},$$

the distinguished element and the successor function. Thus
$0 = \varnothing$, $1 = \{0\}$, $2 = \{0, 1\}$, $3 = \{0, 1, 2\}$, and in general
$n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ is the set of its predecessors.

Let $A$ and $B$ be sets. By
[[lem-ordered-pairs-lie-in-the-double-power-set]] every ordered pair $(a,b)$ with
$a \in A$ and $b \in B$ is an element of $\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B))$, so
[[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]] applied inside that set produces the
**Cartesian product**

$$A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}.$$

Its elements are exactly the ordered pairs $(a,b)$ ([[def-ordered-pair]]) with
$a \in A$ and $b \in B$: no such pair is lost, because each such pair lies in
the ambient set being separated. Thus $z \in A \times B$ holds if and only if
$z = (a,b)$ for some $a \in A$ and some $b \in B$.

Let $\varphi(z, \bar p)$ be a formula of the language of set theory
([[def-language-of-set-theory]]) in which the variable $y$ does not occur free.
The **Separation instance** for $\varphi$ is the sentence

$$\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,\bigl(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p))\bigr).$$

The **Axiom Schema of Separation** is the collection of all these sentences, one
for each such $\varphi$. In words: for any parameters $\bar p$ and any set $x$,
there is a set $y$ whose elements are exactly the elements $z$ of $x$ for which
$\varphi(z,\bar p)$ holds.

It is a schema and not a single axiom because $\varphi$ ranges over the formulas
of the language, of which there are infinitely many, and the language provides no
way to quantify over them.

Let $\varphi(z, w, \bar p)$ be a formula of the language of set theory
([[def-language-of-set-theory]]) in which $A$ and $B$ do not occur free. The
**Replacement instance** for $\varphi$ is the sentence

$$\forall \bar p\,\forall A\,\Bigl(\forall z\,\bigl(z \in A \to \exists! w\,\varphi(z,w,\bar p)\bigr) \to \exists B\,\forall w\,\bigl(w \in B \leftrightarrow \exists z\,(z \in A \wedge \varphi(z,w,\bar p))\bigr)\Bigr).$$

The **Axiom Schema of Replacement** is the collection of all these sentences, one
for each such $\varphi$. In words: if for every $z \in A$ there is exactly one
$w$ with $\varphi(z,w,\bar p)$, then there is a set $B$ whose elements are
exactly those $w$.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Assume the Axiom of Dependent Choice ($\mathrm{DC}$). Let a common-space IVP
interface and bounded time-scheme family be given as in
[[def-common-space-linear-scheme-interface]]. If
the scheme is consistent on its dense invariant subspace, then it is
convergent on every finite time interval if and only if it is stable there,
with stability, consistency, and convergence all measured in the same norm
of $X$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently (property form): if a property $P$ satisfies $P(0)$ and ($P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$) for all $n$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This is the induction principle, the basis of proof by induction.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Since $m=\nu+1$, $\tau_m=m^{-2}>0$ and $\tau_m\to0$ as $\nu\to\infty$. Let $P_m$ be truncation to coordinates $0,\ldots,m-1$ and $R_m$ inclusion. Their norms are at most $1$ by the coordinate supremum estimates and at least $1$ by testing $e_0$, so both have norm $1$ by [F7]. Also $P_mR_m=I_{G_m}$ and $\ker P_m$ is invariant under $U(\tau_m)$ because $U$ is diagonal. The finite maximum $L_m:=\max_{0\le j<m}|1-\tau_mj^2|$ bounds every diagonal multiplier, so $\|Q_mg\|_\infty\le L_m\|g\|_\infty$ and $Q_m$ is bounded. Thus [F2] defines the common-space step $S_m$.

For $j<m$, $0\le1-j^2/m^2\le1$; on coordinates $j\ge m$ the lift uses the multipliers $\exp(-j^2/m^2)\in(0,1]$ from [F3]. Hence every coordinate multiplier of $S_m$ lies in $[0,1]$. Therefore $\|S_mx\|_\infty\le \|x\|_\infty$ for every $x\in c_0$, and [F7] gives $\|S_m\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le1$. The bound $\|S_m^n x\|_\infty\le\|x\|_\infty$ holds at $n=0$; if it holds at $n$, applying the contraction estimate to $S_m^nx$ proves it at $n+1$. Induction [F8] gives it for every $n$, and then [F7] gives $\|S_m^n\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le1$. The family is stable on every finite time interval.

Fix $v\in D$, supported in coordinates $0,\ldots,N$. For $m>N$, direct evaluation and $0<\exp(-r\tau_mj^2)\le1$ give $\max_{\substack{r\in\mathbb N\\r\tau_m\le T}}\frac{\|(S_m-U(\tau_m))U(r\tau_m)v\|_\infty}{\tau_m}\le\|v\|_\infty\max_{0\le j\le N}\frac{|1-\tau_mj^2-\exp(-\tau_mj^2)|}{\tau_m}.$ For $j=0$ the quotient is zero. The maximum of these finitely many quotients tends to zero: for any tolerance choose a threshold for each $j$ (or use threshold $1$ if there is no positive $j$), then take the largest threshold. Multiplication by the fixed $\|v\|_\infty$ preserves this limit. The bound is independent of $r$, so the family is consistent on $D$.
By [F6] and the explicit DC assumption [A1], this consistent stable family converges to the heat semigroup in the common supremum norm, uniformly over grid times in each bounded time interval.

derivations.claim: Let $D$ be the finite-support sequences. By [F4], $X$ is Banach; the identity maps $U(t)=I_X$ form a strongly continuous semigroup with finite-time bound $M_T=1$. By [F5], $D$ is dense and it is invariant under $U$. The positive steps $\tau_m=1/m$ tend to zero, so this is common-space scheme data.

The positive coordinate weights make the displayed maximum a norm: homogeneity and definiteness hold coordinatewise, and the triangle inequality follows by applying the scalar triangle inequality in every coordinate before taking the maximum. The truncation satisfies $\|P_mx\|_{G_m}\le m\|x\|_\infty$, and inclusion satisfies $\|R_mg\|_\infty\le\|g\|_{G_m}$, so both are bounded. Also $P_mR_m=I_{G_m}$ and $\ker P_m$ is invariant under $U=I$. For $g=\sum_{j<m}g_je_j$, the zeroth output coordinate is $g_0+mg_{m-1}$, coordinates $1$ through $m-2$ if present remain $g_j$, and coordinate $m-1$ becomes $0$. Since $|g_0|\le\|g\|_{G_m}$, $m|g_{m-1}|\le\|g\|_{G_m}$, and $|g_j|\le\|g\|_{G_m}$ for $1\le j\le m-2$, it follows that $\|Q_mg\|_{G_m}\le2\|g\|_{G_m}$, including $m=2$. Thus $Q_m$ is bounded and the grid lift [F2] is defined. Also $Q_m^2=Q_m$: it fixes each $e_j$ for $j<m-1$, and $Q_m^2e_{m-1}=Q_m(me_0)=me_0=Q_me_{m-1}$. By induction [F7], $Q_m^n=Q_m$ for every $n\ge1$: the base $n=1$ is immediate, and $Q_m^n=Q_m$ implies $Q_m^{n+1}=Q_mQ_m=Q_m^2=Q_m$. Meanwhile $Q_m^0=I$. Thus the local defect is zero on every $v\in D$ for all sufficiently large $m$, which proves consistency.

For $e_{m-1}$, the lift gives $S_me_{m-1}=m e_0$. Its common-space norm is therefore $m$, while $\|e_{m-1}\|_\infty=1$. Testing this unit vector in [F6] gives $\|S_m\|_{X\to X}\ge m$. For every $T>0$, all sufficiently large $m$ have $\tau_m\le T$, so the common-space family is not stable.
